### HOMECOMING | OCTOBER 2024

![Image 54](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5388a1dfe4b01656e4f9afa2/2ccdd5c3-915f-42ea-a733-88b29f8a6224/Homecoming+3.jpeg)

It’s the time of the year when local high school students have been busy planning and preparing the annual fall celebration of “Homecoming.” Even though many things have changed significantly since the 1950’s when I was in school, many of the homecoming traditions remain the same.

**The Homecoming Parade**…In the early 1950’s, Monticello had only one school building. The high school took up the top floor, and the elementary students were housed in the lower levels. So on Friday afternoon of Homecoming week, ALL the students marched through downtown Monticello. Each high school class had designed a float with a theme to defeat the rival football team. The homecoming royalty was honored by riding in the largest float.

![Image 55](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5388a1dfe4b01656e4f9afa2/5357f953-ab0d-41fe-8347-d824a911ed98/Homecomnig+2.jpeg)

**The Bonfire**…It was a tradition to spend at least a week or two collecting large branches, wood, and a few old tires to make the biggest bonfire possible and locate it near the football field. There were usually a few “guards” whose job it was to make sure someone from a rival school did not burn the bonfire prior to homecoming. On Thursday night prior to the homecoming game, the cheerleaders organized a large pep fest, and then lit the woodpile for the bonfire.

**The Game**…Of course, the whole week was in preparation for the Friday night football game. It was always the most important game of the season to score a win. There was always a large crowd from the community to cheer the team on, and the cheerleaders were there rooting for the team. The high school band played and marched across the field at half time.

![Image 56](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5388a1dfe4b01656e4f9afa2/fada3417-c754-4296-9aae-cfda9ed82728/Homecoming+7+-+Snake+Dance.jpg)

**The Snake Dance**…Immediately after the bonfire, the cheerleaders gathered together, holding hands, and encouraged others to join the line. As students joined the line, it became a long “snake”, and the cheerleaders began to move on. They led the long line through the streets of town, back and forth, in and out of parking lots, still all holding hands. The line moved quickly and sometimes the last section of the line “whipped.” (Injuries sometimes occurred.)

![Image 57](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5388a1dfe4b01656e4f9afa2/5fdfa011-ab5d-458b-b9d7-bc564c4aef91/Homecoming+1.jpeg)

**The Dance**…After the game, there was a dance at the high school gym. The team had cleaned up, the spectators had changed into their fall outfits. Earlier in the week, high school students had voted on a homecoming king and queen, and they had been crowned at an evening ceremony. The dance began with a Grand March led by the homecoming royalty. Phonograph records provided the music, and everyone joined the dance. The Friday dance was the culmination of homecoming for the year.

**Addendum:**

*   In the early years, high school alumnae were encouraged to attend both the game and the dance. Over the years, they have often attended the game, but very seldom have they attended the homecoming dance.

*   The homecoming bonfire has been banned locally for many years for safety reasons.

*   The snake dance often resulted in injuries, so it, too has been banned locally. However, there are many high schools that continue the tradition, but include safety precautions.

### THE BUFFALO HARVEST FESTIVAL | SEPTEMBER 2024

![Image 58](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5388a1dfe4b01656e4f9afa2/e7f1d332-b961-41af-a4f4-fb5b9350cd0a/Buffalo+Days+3.jpg)

Buffalo as a community has been very active in planning and producing a number of activities and events with a variety of interests that bring residents and visitors to the city. Buffalo Days is traditionally held in June, the Kite Festival takes place on frozen Buffalo Lake, and there are a variety of other events during the year.

When I grew up in the 1950’s, I always looked forward to attending a traditional Buffalo community event---the Harvest Festival. With a rural farm theme, the celebration was held late in the summer season, most likely August or September. There were booths set up along Division Street and along 2nd Avenue. Each booth was operated by a local merchant, church, or club. Token gifts such as pencils or rulers were given out as freebies. People could register for prizes at some booths. There were guessing games, too. “_How many jelly beans in the jar?_”

![Image 59](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5388a1dfe4b01656e4f9afa2/7e20f870-7372-4e72-b38d-cd1fd5fb1442/Book+2+%238.jpg)

the Nelsonian being played. From the WC Photo Collection.

One booth encouraged farmers to bring in their tallest stalk of corn. A prize would be given at the end of the Harvest Festival for the winner.

There was a variety of entertainment, also. Along Wide Street, there was an outdoor stage set up. I remember attending a Vaudeville style act by a song and dance man who also told jokes before a crowded audience.

One year, Albert Nelson’s One-Man Band was playing. My dad paid 50 cents for me to enter and watch Mr. Nelson play his instruments.

![Image 60](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5388a1dfe4b01656e4f9afa2/ac0bc5d8-799e-4eb8-83fe-567352c915db/Buffalo+Days.jpg)

Of course, there was the traditional carnival with rides and games. As I remember, the carnival rides were set up in Soo Town and there was a small Ferris wheel across the tracks from the old depot. I had never been on a Ferris wheel, but my big brother, Ted, talked me into my first ride. I was a bit nervous, but got on with Ted by my side. That ride lasted longer than I wanted, and I was relieved to put my feet back on the ground. It was a long time before I was brave enough to try another Ferris wheel ride.

In 1952, the Harvest Festival was replaced by a three day celebration called ‘Buffalo Days.’ It was to be held in July and included 2 parades with bands, outdoor attractions, and Queen Contests. In later years, Buffalo Days has been celebrated in early June.

We like to remember the Harvest Festival, but today, we always look forward to the next Buffalo Days celebration.

### SUNSET GROVE RESORTS | AUGUST 2024

Early in the 1900’s, Pulaski Lake was known for its pristine spring-fed water and excellent fishing. Several resorts were established, mostly on the south and west sides of the lake. The east side of the lake had very high banks, was wooded, and was bordered by rich farmland.

My grandfather, Harry Kopff, born in 1861, grew up in Beaver Dam, Wisconsin where he spent his youth hunting and fishing. Beaver Dam Lake was 20 miles long, and a few miles away was Horicon Marsh, well-known as a wildlife refuge and waterfowl sanctuary. Harry had learned that Minnesota was also good for hunting and fishing. So, at age 34, he borrowed his father’s team of horses and a wagon and made the trip to Minnesota. He stayed for a while in Monticello, then became acquainted with the fishing and hunting prospects around Pulaski Lake.

Soon, he met my grandmother, Grace Varner, who lived on a farm on the west side of Pulaski Lake. In 1899, Grace and Harry were married. She was 16… he was 38! Harry bought a few acres just east of Buffalo on what is now County 35 and built a small home there. He and Grace raised raspberries for the local market. In the next five years, Grace gave birth to three girls. Then, in about 1904, Harry purchased a few acres on the east side of Pulaski Lake, built a small home and moved his family there. Soon, a fourth child was born, a son named Spencer.

Harry and Grace continued to grow raspberries, but Harry spent much time fishing on Pulaski Lake and also on Buffalo Lake. He would pack his catch in a big barrel with ice from the local ice house and cart the barrel to the Buffalo train depot. From there, it went by rail to Eisenminger’s Store in St. Paul where there was a good market for fresh fish. Customers in St. Paul would ask where those large crappies and sunfish came from, and soon there were people wanting to fish the Wright County lakes for themselves.

![Image 61](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5388a1dfe4b01656e4f9afa2/60125ec9-51c2-486d-8419-91faed1781f5/Sunset+Cove+2.jpg)

**The main house at the Sunset Grove Resort…ca.1940**

In 1912, Harry received word from Wisconsin that his father had died and left him a small inheritance. He used the money to build a small rental cottage for a family interested in spending the summer at the lake. Over the next few years, he built more cottages, and eventually he had six, each with a small acreage and a boat to use. Harry and Grace named their venture the “Sunset Grove Resort.” People familiar with the resort just called it ‘the Grove.’ Most families who rented a cottage would come back summer after summer. Some came by car; others came by train to Buffalo and were transported to the resort by local draymen.

None of the cottages had running water at first. There were outhouses available. A community pump was situated in the center of the resort. Eventually, electricity was installed in the cottages. Grace had grown up in a family known for their good pastries, and she often made pies and cakes…often requested by the summer residents.

Harry and Grace and five children lived in the main house at Sunset Grove. The home consisted of one long great room, a small bedroom, and a kitchen with a few cabinets and a small table. There was also a separate cupboard that stood against one wall where Grace kept supplies. In the center of the kitchen, there was a trap door in the floor. A ladder was in place to climb down into a small dirt cellar. There were a few shelves in the cellar where Grace kept her canned goods and vegetables from the garden. Harry had built a screen porch on the lake side of the house to catch the evening breeze. In the summer, Spencer slept on the porch, often waking up with a few sprinkles of rain in his face.

During the Prohibition era, there was an additional perk for the summer residents. Directly across the road to the east, there was an old farmhouse owned by a resident farmer---known as ‘Unk’ by the locals. He built a still in his upstairs bedroom. You read about him back in the June post (see below).

![Image 62](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5388a1dfe4b01656e4f9afa2/6211b45f-230a-4efb-8b45-450a025db943/Sunset+Cove+1.jpg)

**What was once the Sunset Grove Resort is now a residential neighborhood called Sunset Cove.**

Harry and Grace raised their family at the lake, and soon each of the three girls left home to find work or go to school. Their son earned cash doing odd jobs for some of the local farmers. But Spencer and his dad often packed a lunch and walked several miles to explore new hunting or fishing grounds.

In February of 1932, Harry was out on the north east side of Pulaski Lake hoping to catch a few fish through the ice. It was cold and, nearby, there were two intersecting pressure cracks in the ice. Snow covered the cracks. Harry happened to walk over the spot where the cracks intersected. He fell through the ice. Nearby fishermen were not able to pull him out, and he drowned.

Grace and her son, Spencer, maintained the resort for a few more years, but Grace became ill and died in 1946. The resort was divided into lots and sold.

The era of small summer cottages on Pulaski Lake was about over. Many of the residents who had spent their summers at Sunset Grove purchased the lots and enjoyed several more summers at the lake. Since then, each lot has been sold to families that have built beautiful year-round homes. The high bank has been cut down for a better view with updated landscaping. The residents in that neighborhood have renamed Grace’s “Sunset Grove” as Sunset Cove.

### WRIGHT COUNTY FAIR DISAPPOINTMENTS | JULY 2024

It’s Wright County Fair time! As a youngster, that always brought excitement to our family. My brother and I were members of a 4-H Club and my mother was one of the leaders. We spent many hours preparing for the fair…sewing, cooking, grooming animals…then loading everything into our car for the hour-long trek to Howard Lake. Even though I had many successful experiences at the fair, the mistakes and disappointments were the most memorable.

My first disappointment was during one summer in the early 1950’s. Our exhibits were ready, the car was loaded, and we were about to leave for Howard Lake. My mother received a phone call from a friend who said that there was polio diagnosed in a person near Howard Lake. Regrettably, we didn’t get to the fair that year.

Later, when I was nine years old, I worked for several weeks hand sewing a set of pot holders and hemming a dish towel. My stitches were perfectly spaced, tiny and even. I thought I would get a blue ribbon…I received a white ribbon (lowest prize)...very discouraging for me.

![Image 63](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5388a1dfe4b01656e4f9afa2/10c48ac2-91f7-454e-98ba-b46af672cab1/Polio+4.jpg)

Another year, when I was about 10 years old, I decided to take a young sheep to the fair. That would have required me to spend lots of time with Wooly. I did work with her at times. We trimmed and blocked her wool, but when it was time to bring Wooly into the show ring, Wooly panicked and ran out of the ring and down the hallway. My big brother had to leave his own sheep to get Wooly back into his pen. That was the last animal that I brought to the fair.

In 4-H, there were many competitive events prior to the fair. One of them was a silent demonstration on how to make a pie. By the time I was 12, I had made many pies, so I knew the process very well. The event was held at the old Buffalo High School on one hot July day. I brought my bowl, rolling pin, bread board, and pie crust ingredients to the school. I began mixing and rolling the crust…and soon ended up with a sticky mess! Other participants knew enough to bring lots of ice on a hot July day. My lard had melted on that hot July day. It was a good learning experience for me.

![Image 64](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5388a1dfe4b01656e4f9afa2/de6a0813-3ef7-4466-b017-14fcdfc380c4/Polio+3.jpg)

One project that went pretty well for me was when I sewed a dress for myself, modeled it, and then entered it at the county fair. I received an honorable mention for modeling, a purple ribbon for the sewing, and it was taken to the MN State Fair for judging. However, it received a 4th place ribbon at the State because the zipper’s color did not match the exact color of the dress. Again, I was disappointed in that 4th place ribbon.

There were lots of other experiences in 4-H at the fair. I have good memories of working at the food stand, making new friends, and always learning from my successes and my failures.

**_Addendum: Polio Epidemics_**

![Image 65](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5388a1dfe4b01656e4f9afa2/911dd70e-500f-4a03-a354-6a7c111f32de/Polio+1.jpg)

_In the 1940’s and 1950’s, there were several polio epidemics throughout the United States. In 1946, the Minnesota State Fair was cancelled because of polio. In 1952, there were 3,145 deaths from polio in the United States._

_Polio was a fearful disease. The disease developed suddenly, usually during summer months, and struck children more often than adults. People were terrified that they or their children would die or be paralyzed for life._

_Our family lived as many other families did. We stayed away from places where people gathered and kept abreast of any new polio outbreaks._

_Then, a polio vaccine was developed by Jonas Salk and licensed in 1955. In 1957, mass immunizations were promoted by the March of Dimes. I remember standing in line at the Monticello High School to receive my sugar cube containing the Salk vaccine._

### MOONSHINE HENRY | JUNE 2024

![Image 66](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5388a1dfe4b01656e4f9afa2/9c1da16a-29f2-440f-a1c1-60400760a2b7/Moonshine+2.jpg)

My grandparents had a small resort on the east side of Lake Pulaski that they named “Sunset Grove.” They rented small cottages to families for a summer retreat. Each cottage included the use of a boat and access to the lake. There was another perk that a few of the summer residents learned to enjoy… regular social activities at the old farmhouse on the hill across the road.

This was in the early 1920s and on into the 1930s. The Prohibition Law had been passed in 1920, so liquor could not be sold legally.

So all across the country, folks took advantage of people’s thirst for liquor, and established illegal liquor production. In that little old farmhouse on the hill, Henry Ordorff constructed a ‘still’ in his upstairs bedroom. Friends and neighbors spread the word, and soon Henry had a booming business. Some customers hung out at the farm and soon it also became a “party house.”

Eventually, word spread that liquor was available at Henry’s, and he even attracted some cronies from the Chicago and St. Paul racketeers. They needed a place to hide out when the law was in pursuit.

My father was a teenager at the time, living across the road, but also working odd jobs in the area. He and his mother sometimes walked up the hill to Henry’s if there was music or a party was going on. So my dad had lots of stories to tell.

Customers of Henry’s sometimes had too much moonshine and needed a breather. They would walk down to the lake through Sunset Grove in order to cool off--- (occasionally making the trek in the nude).

One regular customer was a St. Paul policeman by the name of Jim. He and his wife were summer residents at Sunset Grove. Jim was one of those people that became incorrigible with too much to drink. One afternoon at Henry’s, he had been drinking too much and suddenly wanted to fist-punch everyone in sight. My grandmother quickly hid under the porch, and others scattered out into the woods. Jim began fist-punching the nearest tree until he passed out.

Another time, there was a group of men enjoying a glass or two of moonshine. One man slipped a “knock-out” drop into another man’s drink. The victim slowly became sleepy and eventually passed out. Whatever cash was in the victim’s pocket disappeared. The knock-out drop was a little too strong, and the victim later died. Authorities were notified, and Henry spent some time in the county jail. He was later released and returned to continue with his business.

There were many more tales about the events at the old house on the hill, but in 1933, the Prohibition law was repealed, and Henry’s moonshine days were over.

Henry continued living in that old farmhouse. He had a large steam engine that he operated during threshing season at many of the local farms. In the mid-1950s, he became ill and spent time in a nursing home. He died in 1957.

![Image 67](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5388a1dfe4b01656e4f9afa2/ca59d163-a5b1-48e9-9d7c-ab98ec9a5e99/moonshine+1.jpg)

**Afterword:**That old house became available for purchase when Henry went to a nursing home. My dad’s oldest sister, Clara, lived on a neighboring farm and was married to Henry’s nephew. She purchased the house and a number of acres in 1956. My father, who was a carpenter, helped Clara clean the place up, renovated the home, modernized it with electricity and plumbing, and made it into a comfortable old farmhouse. The upstairs bedroom still had a few of the fixtures that Henry used to make his moonshine!

The old house is still on the hill (2022). Sometime in the 1980’s, that house and a few acres were sold to a young couple who resided there for several years. The rest of the farm has seen great changes. It is now the site of a residential development called GREENBRIAR Estates.

### MAY TRADITIONS | MAY 2024

![Image 68](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5388a1dfe4b01656e4f9afa2/0077b840-bcc6-4875-81ad-cb5da299bded/mayday+5.jpg)

As a student in my little country school, I always looked forward to May 1…we called it May Day.

Prior to May Day, students in my country school spent all of our spare time cutting, folding, and pasting colored paper to form May baskets. Some of us were brave enough to actually fill the baskets, sneak up to a friend’s home, hang the basket, knock on the door, then run like a deer so we didn’t get caught. (A few of us actually wanted to get caught.) It was all in fun… a way to celebrate spring and the end of a long winter.

![Image 69](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5388a1dfe4b01656e4f9afa2/173798ef-d47b-48ce-bcea-15d50a8558cc/mayday+2.jpg)

Historically, the origin of May Day goes back to early European pagan festivities. The first of May was the most important day of the year because it was the return of spring vegetation and the end of the dark, cold winter months. People in many European countries and some areas in the United States, still celebrate spring by dancing around the May Pole.

Back at our country school after our May Day excursions, we found many ways to enjoy spring. At recess, we played softball or organized other games like “Pump, Pump, Pull away” or “Red Rover.” Our teacher took us on educational hikes to Cedar Lake or Bertram Lake. We watched for bluebirds or meadow larks. We learned how to identify poison ivy and watched for early signs of trillium and jack-in-the pulpits.

![Image 70](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5388a1dfe4b01656e4f9afa2/b37b7b34-6db4-4d29-95e8-5bd101a3149c/mayday+4.jpg)

In school, there was always a Mother’s Day project as a gift for our mothers. One year, we made and painted a small plaster statue of a bear to mount on the wall. At home, around Mother’s Day, our family scoured the woods for morels…the spring mushroom.

The end of May brought a burst of lilac blooms in every farmyard. But it also brought the last day of school. Students had worked hard cleaning out their desks, scrubbing the chalkboards, and tidying the classroom. Older students had raked the lawn. To celebrate the end of school, parents brought a pot luck lunch. After lunch, there was more fun…wheelbarrow races, three-legged races, tug-of-war...all with small prizes. The day ended with a softball game…sometimes with parents participating.

May was over. Summer was just beginning. We looked forward to days of fishing, swimming in the local lakes, and playing hide-and-seek in the corn fields. Life was good!

![Image 71](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5388a1dfe4b01656e4f9afa2/514eae77-c134-4ca7-b1e0-63d5ce123b21/maypole+6.jpg)

### WHEN WILL THE FLIVVER SINK? | APRIL 2024

![Image 72](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5388a1dfe4b01656e4f9afa2/6e04d03a-45bf-4ac6-b6e6-e8de77fce197/Flivver+Sink+clipping.jpg)

One event that occurred each winter in Monticello was the breaking up of the ice on the Mississippi River. It usually happened about the middle of April, but varied greatly according to the weather.

Each year, there was a guessing game played out in the community connected with the ‘ice out’ on the river. One of the local community organizations would place an old car on the river ice. To retrieve the car after sinking, a heavy chain would be attached to the car. Lottery tickets would be sold and each person buying a ticket would write down their guess as to the date and time that the old car would sink into the river. A nice prize was awarded to the ticket holder with the closest guess. As the weather warmed up, there was much speculation and conversation as to when that ‘flivver’ was going down.

In connection with the spring melt, many people would walk across the bridge to watch the huge chunks of ice float downstream; some ice chunks had trees and other debris atop them. As those chunks would collide with the support piers below, the whole bridge would shake like it was going to collapse. It was always a thrill to take that walk across the old bridge.

My husband, Karl, tells me that some of the brave local teenagers would climb out on the girders under the bridge to the third pier. That was the pier that would shake the most when a large hunk of ice would hit it. (I really don’t know how Karl knows those details.) What teenagers wouldn’t do for a thrill!!!

Eventually, the flivver event was discontinued because of the environmental impact of a car sinking in the river. The opening of the power plant upstream resulted in an open river with very little ice forming along the city.

### VARNERS IN THE CIVIL WAR | March 2024

![Image 73](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5388a1dfe4b01656e4f9afa2/82383d3e-c592-4dcc-9a2c-e5d16e20e273/Varners+CC+1.jpg)

I recently attended the Interesting presentation about the soldiers from Wright County who enlisted and formed Company E, serving in the Civil War. I began thinking about my own Varner ancestors who also served in the Civil War.

There were six Varner brothers who migrated from Pennsylvania to Wright County before and after the Civil War: John, Lafayette, David, Henry, Jacob, and Solomon. They were farmers and some had other skilled occupations, such as a cooper, carpenter, and potter. They all purchased farms north and west of Buffalo. They worked hard clearing the land and raised large families.

![Image 74](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5388a1dfe4b01656e4f9afa2/c67beafc-9a5a-4e30-bcbf-b3d6ef3b6f39/Varners+CC+2.jpg)

While still in Pennsylvania, three of the brothers, John, Lafayette and David, enlisted together in the Union Army. They were inducted into Company K, 4th Pennsylvania Cavalry in February of 1864.

John Varner, my great grandfather, received a $200 bounty to volunteer. Before leaving, on February 28, 1864, he married Frances Hickman. Together, John, Lafayette, and David left Pennsylvania for Virginia where they took part in a number of battles including Stony Creek, Ream’s Station, and the Appomattox Campaign. All three brothers survived the Civil War. They served in the Cavalry for 1 ½ years and were mustered out on July 1, 1865.

![Image 75](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5388a1dfe4b01656e4f9afa2/86a425b3-d80a-4772-b5a8-1975d67db9dd/Varners+CC+3.jpg)

In November of 1865, while he was serving under General Phillip Sheridan at the Battle of Stony Creek, John Varner became a father. Back home in Pennsylvania, Frances had given birth to a son…William Sheridan Varner. His middle name was chosen in honor of General Sheridan.

**Addendum:** Shortly after returning to Pennsylvania, John and his young family joined several of his brothers who had settled in Buffalo, Minnesota. He purchased a farm on the west side of Pulaski Lake where 10 more children were born. As the oldest child, William Sheridan Varner did much of the clearing of the land. Later, he became well- known as a builder of homes and commercial buildings around Wright County. He was known as “Sherd Varner.”

_(The Varner families were very prolific. There are hundreds of Varner descendants today in Wright County… and many more throughout the world. If you live in Wright County, you probably know a Varner descendant.)_

### CREAMERY DAY | february 2024

_A free meal and an afternoon of entertainment…an annual community event prior to 1960 in towns throughout Wright County. We called it Creamery Day._

Up until about 1960, Wright County had many small towns. Much of the commerce depended on farm communities. Many of the towns had creameries. Dairy farmers brought in their milk to be made into butter or processed into other dairy products. Downtown businesses stocked their stores with items essential to the needs of local residents.

![Image 76](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5388a1dfe4b01656e4f9afa2/065ebb0f-3fd0-4390-a7c7-a186a56f018d/Monti+Creamery.jpg)

As a member of a Monticello farm family, I grew up attending our local Creamery Day.

Each spring, local farm leaders organized a community get-together at the local high school gymnasium. Local businesses served a free lunch to all who attended. It was a way for them to say “thank you” for the local trade. It was also a way for the farmers and the “townies” to mingle.

On the food trays, there were sausages, cheese sandwiches, potato salad, cookies, Dixie cups of ice cream, milk, coffee, and more. While the meal was being served, the high school band played several numbers. (Band members also received a trip through the food line.)

By about 2 o’clock in the afternoon, the tables had been cleaned up, the stage was cleared, and people had taken their seats in anticipation of the rest of the afternoon. Sometimes there was a short business meeting by the local Co-operative Creamery Board. A speaker might be asked to present new ideas on farm topics. Then came the entertainment. There might be a musical group, a comedian, a juggler, or a magician. The day ended about 4 o’clock, except for a few stragglers who took the opportunity for a quick visit with friends and neighbors.

One of the attendees one year was Senator Hubert Humphrey who never passed the opportunity to speak to a crowd. After he was introduced, I remember him looking through the crowd and recognizing people by name who he had met at some prior gathering.

Creamery Days were discontinued sometime in the 1960’s. As communities have grown and changed, people have found other opportunities for public get-togethers, but thoughts of those Creamery Days evoke good memories of small town traditions.

### FROST SHIELDS | JANUARY 2024

_Some of you might remember riding in an automobile that had a poor (or no) heater or defroster. In the winter, the windows would have so much frost on them that it would be unsafe to drive._

Car owners could stop at their local service station and purchase “frost shields” for the windows. They were made of clear heavy plastic and the edges had heavy felt glued onto the plastic. The service station attendant would install the frost shield, but the car had to be warmed up first, and the windows had to be clean and dry. Once installed, the view was frost free.

The problem with the frost shield was that they sometimes sprung a leak and let in frosty air. Also, when summer came, they got in the way for opening the windows. So they only lasted for one season.

### COLD WEATHER Memories | December 2023

_Brrr!! The cold weather is on its way. But it brings back memories of the many ways we dealt with cold when I was a child on the farm._

The farmhouse did not have central heat. It was kept warm by a furnace in the basement and two heat registers…one in the kitchen and one in the central dining room. To save heat, the living room was closed up for the winter months. We had a wood cook stove that provided a warm cozy kitchen early in the morning. Each evening, my grandmother, who lived with us, would place a brick or a flat iron on the cook stove to heat up before bedtime. The brick would be wrapped in a towel and placed between flannel sheets at the foot of the bed. We would crawl in and cover up with two or three wool quilts. The brick could be unwrapped for more heat as it cooled down.

![Image 79](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5388a1dfe4b01656e4f9afa2/9b885ffa-984b-4bc4-b0c4-679fb59b05eb/WC+60-025+copy+Rockford+Blizzard+1916-17.jpg)

The fire in the basement furnace was nearly out by the time my dad got up in the morning, so he had to go down to stoke the fire. The house was still cold when it was time for me to get ready for school. My mother had my clothes warming near the kitchen wood range. I dressed in layers--- underclothes, then long brown stockings (held up with a garter belt), next, my brother’s old long johns, a cotton shirt and wool sweater, and an extra pair of socks and shoes. Before going to school, there were overshoes, snow pants, a warm coat, knit hat, mittens, and a long wool scarf that wrapped around my neck and mouth.

In the summer, we walked the 1½ miles to school, but in the winter, we usually had a ride. My dad or the neighbor would drive us in their car if the roads were plowed. If there was snow, the neighbor would hitch up his team of horses, hook up his sleigh, and pick us up, stop at the corner for the teacher, and continue on to school. To stay warm on the ride, my mother placed a hot brick near our feet and covered our laps with a wool blanket.

Arriving at school, the neighbor helped get the wood furnace going. We kept our coats on until the room warmed up, and sat near the front of the room where the big stove was located. The cloak room was frigid, so any water in the basin was frozen solid. When the older boys arrived at school, they used the hand pump in the entryway to obtain water for the day.

Those are happy memories, but I’m glad they are memories. I much prefer central heat, electric blankets, warm automobile seats, and heated steering wheels.

### ON LABOR DAY, THOUGHTS OF SCHOOL | SEPTEMBER 2026

Labor Day---the end of summer, and for a family of teachers, it was the weekend to get ready for the first day of school. Labor Day always reminds me of my mother who taught in four different Wright County rural schools.

![Image 4: Image of teacher Mabel Shaw](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5388a1dfe4b01656e4f9afa2/30c4ee4a-4b6e-4b38-9551-43b53e7d7c6e/Mabel+Shaw.jpg)

Image of Mabel Shaw

Mabel Shaw grew up in rural Buffalo, then roomed in town so she could attend high school, and graduated in 1924. Next, she attended “Normal School” teacher training, held at Buffalo High School, for about 9 months to prepare her for teaching in the rural schools.

She was soon assigned to a school north of Buffalo. With no means of transportation, teaching jobs included room and board at one of the local homes. She told of rolling over snowdrifts to get to school, then starting a fire in the wood furnace each morning. Her salary was about $40 a month and was reduced a bit during the Depression years. Even so, she was eventually able to purchase a Model T. She learned how to change oil, fix a tire and how to replace a head on the engine.

Over the years, Mom shared how teaching in a country school was very different than teaching in schools of today.

![Image 5: Image of Mabel Shaw's class of children sitting for a group picture](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5388a1dfe4b01656e4f9afa2/dd3113c6-11ec-4d0d-9837-d85e535ce8d0/Shaw+Class.jpg)

Working with eight grades, the older students taught the younger ones. The young students listened in on geography and arithmetic lessons for the older students. Learning was a co-operative affair. Students kept the firewood stocked and helped clean the schoolroom.

Memorizing poems or important facts was common. Names of the U.S. presidents, the state capitals, the Gettysburg address…all might be assigned to memorize.

![Image 6: Image of printing alphabet exercise](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5388a1dfe4b01656e4f9afa2/127a3c75-0678-4f7a-b7e6-52fbd7d87839/Shaw+Class+Project.jpg)

Printing was not taught. First grade students learned cursive writing. The Palmer method required penmanship drills to perfect handwriting.

Manual art was included for the boys at school. Teacher manuals included directions on making breadboards, building birdhouses, designing yard art, sharpening saws. It was an early form of industrial arts (and a way to keep the boys busy).

The teacher worked for several months at preparing eighth grade students for the state board exams. Tests were difficult, and the teacher’s job was to see that the student passed the exam.

A county superintendent visited all the rural schools regularly. He checked to see that things were working, children were attending school and learning. Each teacher was assigned to a school for 3 or 4 years. After that, the teacher moved to a different rural school so that children had the opportunity to learn from a different teacher.

After teaching for 11 years, in 1936 my mother resigned to get married. At that time, married women were not allowed to teach. (She could be taking a job away from a man!) That changed during WW II when so many men left to join the military. Many female teachers went back to teaching. My mother did not.

However, she never stopped teaching. She helped her children and grandchildren learn the names of the birds and wildflowers. She became a 4-H leader and encouraged quality participation in whatever club members chose to do. Teaching came naturally.

### REMEBERING THE THRESHING

This past summer, during all the construction on Highway 25, I had the opportunity to drive along many of the township roads where farmers were busy in their ‘amber fields of grain.’ Huge combines were busily moving through expansive crops of wheat and oats. I couldn’t help comparing this harvest to the days of threshing that I remembered from the farm of my childhood.

![Image 7: image of old thresher](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5388a1dfe4b01656e4f9afa2/6dba7154-7f0c-418b-b33d-0bc03fbb6ad0/thresher.jpg)

Threshing (or “trashing” as many of my neighbors called it) happened when the ripe grain turned a beautiful golden amber. Neighborhood farmers gathered together to complete the harvest---rotating the work at each farm according to which crop was ready. Grain had already been cut into bundles using a grain binder pulled by a tractor, then arranged in ‘shocks’ to dry in the fields.

In our neighborhood, there was one farmer who owned a huge black steam engine along with a threshing machine. He lived about ¾ mile away from our farm. When the steam engine was on its way, you could hear it coming, but it would take another ½ hour or more to get to our farm. After arriving, the set-up and organizing began. Neighbors had arrived with tractors and wagons. Farmers brought their young sons to help. Labor jobs were assigned according to experience. Men and boys drove the tractors to the grain fields, used pitchforks to load the bundles of grain onto the wagons. When loaded, the wagon was taken to the work site where the bundles were pitched into the thresher. The kernels of grain were separated and the straw was blown through a large cylinder out into a pile…soon to become a huge straw stack. The grain was loaded into a wagon to be transferred into the granary.

While the men and boys worked at harvesting the grain, my mother and grandmother were busy cooking in the kitchen. On the previous day, Grandma had baked a batch of homemade bread, Mom had made several pies. Early in the morning, a beef roast or several chickens were being roasted, potatoes were peeled, boiled and mashed, and several kinds of vegetables were prepared. My job was to get the long table ready with plates, silverware, butter, salt and pepper.

![Image 8: Poster for Nowthen Threshing show](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5388a1dfe4b01656e4f9afa2/128053da-56bf-42db-b9af-cac3174d9fa6/Nowthen+Event.png)

At noon, the machines were shut down, and seven to nine hungry men and boys arrived at the back door. Outside, a basin had been set up along with a hose of running water. Hands were washed and the hose was used to cool and freshen the work crew.

It didn’t take long for the gang to find a seat at the table and dig in. They made quick work of the food that was on the table. After a short rest, the guys went back to work. When the harvest on our farm was complete, the machines and crew went on to the next farm, each family sharing the work as the harvesting continued.

Farmers always looked forward to threshing. It gave neighbors a chance to work together, visit a bit, and help each other to complete their harvest.

**A Side Note:**My father always came home with a report of what was served for dinner at each of the farms where he was part of the crew. It almost seemed that there might have been an unofficial competition as to which wife fixed the best meal. I always wonder what the other guys said of the meals that were prepared at our home.

**Coming Event:** In case you would like to see grain being harvested, you can attend the Nowthen Threshing Show. One of the Wright County Historical Society board members, Mary Wetter, is involved with her family and others in producing that event.

### OLD BUFFALO HIGH SCHOOL | JULY 2026

![Image 9](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5388a1dfe4b01656e4f9afa2/fa3152b6-b27b-420a-806a-8a74bdc1d4cb/Old+Buff+HS+2.jpg)

Fire escape similar to Buffalo HS

Some of my earliest memories are from random experiences at the building from which my mom graduated in 1924…the old Buffalo High School (now remodeled into Discovery Elementary). In the 1950’s that building was impressively large. There were a number of steps to get to the entry door. After entering, I always looked for that big frightening bison head mounted overhead in the lobby. Off to the side there was a large portrait of a smiling man. (I believe he was a well-loved janitor.) Straight ahead and through the doors was the auditorium with theater seats and a balcony. At Christmas time, Santa would always make an entrance on the stage, greet everyone, and then we would stand in line to get our bag of Christmas treats.

Later, when I became a 4-H member, there were county-wide meetings in the auditorium and in some of the classrooms. As part of our food preparation 4-H project, a friend and I had prepared a team demonstration on how to properly set a table. At age nine, we used our dolly dishes, set up a card table with a tablecloth. We practiced our demonstration many times over, then presented it for the judges at the school. It went well, but we only received a red (2nd prize) ribbon. (Good experience, though!)

My first speech was given in that auditorium at Buffalo High School. At age 14, I had earned a three-day trip to 4-H camp at Itaska Park. I was asked to give a review of my camp experience at the annual awards night. After much nervous preparation and a lot of practice in front of a mirror, my brief presentation for a couple hundred people went off well…whew!!!

As a student at Monticello High School in the 1950’s, I sometimes attended basketball games between Buffalo and Monticello team rivals. In those days, the Buffalo home games were played right there in the Buffalo auditorium. The curtains were pulled back from the stage, because the basketball court was behind the stage. Seating was set up around the court as well as next to the stage area. It became crowded at times, but we still enjoyed the competition.

![Image 10](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5388a1dfe4b01656e4f9afa2/80eef63e-6548-48e2-b865-bfb15ed1e7a2/Old+Buff+HS+1.jpg)

Advertisement for the Buffalo Milky Way

The most interesting part of that old Buffalo High School building was a large metal tube (about 3 feet in diameter) outside at the north end of the building. The top end of the tube was attached to a door on the second story. The tube came down at an angle next to the building and ended up on the ground. I believe the tube was a fire escape. (I can only imagine how many neighborhood kids explored that tube and found their way to the top of that fire escape!)

Next to the Buffalo High School, there was a small building near the street in the shape of a Quonset hut. It was an ice cream/candy/convenience store. I believe it was called ‘The Milky Way.’ It was located at the northeast corner of 1st Avenue and 2nd Street. At age 5, I made my first purchase there…a nickel package of Juicy Fruit gum!

All good memories of my mom’s alma mater!

### TASTES OF SPRING | JUNE 2026

![Image 11: picture of lady slippers](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5388a1dfe4b01656e4f9afa2/90d43a1e-28b0-4d8f-9573-a1a4962c39a6/flower1.jpg)

One of the things we look forward to after a long Minnesota winter is watching for signs of spring…the beautiful apple and cherry blossoms, the first robin, and early dandelion sprouts. Each spring, Grandma would take her sharp kitchen knife and go out foraging for the first tender dandelion leaves. We all looked forward to her dandelion/bacon salad---it was a delicious spring treat.

Childhood memories bring thoughts of family traditions that illustrate how much we enjoyed the coming of spring. On one of those beautiful early April days, Mom would load Grandma and me into our ’38 Ford and take a drive to look for pussy willows and Pasque flowers. Later, we would tour the country lanes scanning the ditches for wild asparagus. (Asparagus grows wild along old roadways and is especially abundant near cemeteries. Well-established asparagus plants grow thick and tender.)

Another spring ritual was a hike into the deep woods---always on the lookout for anemones, trilliums, or jack-in-the pulpits. Along the way, we might find a few wild onions to add to our dinner salad. I always looked forward to finding a honeysuckle flower…a sweet taste while enjoying the hike.

After I had my own family, we would often forage through the woods looking for morel mushrooms. My father’s advice was always.to look for them “when the oak leaves are the size of squirrel’s ears.” He also advised that morels often grew near a dead elm tree. After my son was a teenager, his Mother’s Day tradition was to take his mother out to hunt for morel mushrooms. Afterward, we would enjoy a grilled hamburger smothered in sauteed mushrooms (if we were lucky enough to find some!).

Soon we will look forward in June to the first strawberries. Our Minnesota strawberries make delicious strawberry jam and the best strawberry shortcake.

Those early tastes of spring only last a short time. We’ll enjoy them while we can, and we’ll look forward to them again in coming springs.

### BEACON LIGHT NEAR BUFFALO | APRIL 2026

![Image 17](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5388a1dfe4b01656e4f9afa2/6bc98dd7-7bf1-40ad-abc6-675b45d81533/Beacon+Light+-CC.jpg)

When I was a little girl living on the farm, we often would travel to Buffalo to visit relatives. As we approached the city, I would always look for the beacon light. The light was located atop a tall tower, and the beam seemed to travel across the sky as we drove past. At times it seemed to blink off and on. That tower was located very close to the present location of West Pulaski Park. I later learned that at one time there was a landing strip for airplanes located nearby---on the west side of Highway 25 (close to the present location of the Wright County Government Center).

Recently, I decided to do some research on the beacon light. This is what I found:

**_In 1918, the U.S. Post Office initiated air mail service between the East and West Coasts. Airplanes had open cockpits, and pilots relied on their personal vision for navigation. Prompt mail delivery was important, so pilots would fly in all kinds of weather and often flew through the night. Sometimes pilots would lose their way or crash._**

**_In the 1920’s and 1930’s, to improve airplane safety, the U. S. Government put up a series of beacon lights, located about 10 miles apart, that would be used as a guide for planes across the country. Each beacon was mounted on a tall tower and had a powerful rotating light to make it visible to pilots flying at night. The lights often flashed with Morse code to signal information to the pilots. Many of the towers had very large cement arrows installed on the ground to point the way during the day._**

**_By 1933, the US Airway Beacon System consisted of more that 1,500 beacons across about 18,000 miles guiding pilots through the skies at night._**

**_By the 1940’s, airplane technology had progressed significantly. Radio communication and instrument use replaced the beacon lights. Eventually, most towers were torn down. There are still a few beacon towers in use in Montana. Some small airports still use a beacon light system. In Mounds Park, St. Paul, MN, a beacon tower has been installed as a reminder of one that existed there at the early part of the 20th Century._**

I would be interested to hear if anyone else in Wright County remembers the beacon light. Let us know!

### RECYCLING AT WCHS | MARCH 2026

Our town board recently renewed the recycling service to provide much larger bins to be picked up just once a month. That works well for me, but others have expressed complaints---not often enough---bins too big to handle, etc.

So, I began to wonder about the history of recycling. When did we find it necessary to pay someone to recycle our stuff? My thoughts went back to my grandmother. She would have been crowned the “Queen of Recycling.” Nothing went to waste in our home!

Boxes of dry cereal always had a waxed inner package. Grandma saved that waxed paper for wrapping the sandwiches in our school lunch boxes. (Plastic bags were not yet available.)

Grandma went through the mail each day, cut out the blank part of any white envelope or junk mail, stacked up the pieces, then inserted a large safety pin in the corner, hung the stack on a nail to serve as a notepad.

The ends of flour sacks came with a heavy string binding. That string had to be wound up and saved for later use.

Flour sacks were made into aprons. Worn clothing was cut up to be made into quilts. Buttons were cut off and placed in a metal container for later use.

![Image 18](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5388a1dfe4b01656e4f9afa2/3805ee3c-5924-481e-a2e4-3cb26f46128a/candied+orange.jpg)

Fruit peels were not thrown away. Orange peels were candied for use in cakes and cookies. Watermelon rinds were made into watermelon pickles. Onion skins were saved to be used at Easter time. Eggs were boiled together with the onion skins to make colored eggs.

Large juice cans were used as containers for fresh milk from the farm. Table scraps, eggshells, coffee grounds were saved in a large can for chicken feed.

If milk turned sour, Grandma didn’t throw it out…she made cottage cheese!

Grandma mixed bacon fat, eggs, table scraps, and ground grain from the barn to make a baked cake for our pet dogs.

Grandma had a big garden. She raised several kinds of beans. Each fall, she made sure to allow her beans to ripen. She dried the seeds, placed them in ‘used’ envelopes, labeled them, and stored them in her top dresser drawer for the next spring’s planting.

The first plastic bag in our home was a large one with advertising from a seed company. Homemade bread was kept in that bag. It was washed and dried often but lasted several years before its usefulness was ended.

I wonder what Grandma would say if she could see all the “useful stuff” that we place into those big recycling bins.

### NICHOLAS SILVIUS IN THE REVOLUTIONARY WAR | FEBRUARY 2026

This year, the United States of America is celebrating its 250th anniversary. The PBS television stations have replayed the Ken Burns’ documentary of the American Revolution. For many viewers, it sparked a thought, “Do I have any ancestors that participated in the Revolutionary War?” And that is when I did a little research… “Yes, I do; this is the story of my connection to an ancestor who fought in the Revolutionary War:”

Nicholas Silvius was born to German immigrant parents on January 15, 1743, in Lehigh Township, Bucks Co. PA. He had 5 siblings. In 1755, he and his younger sister, Anna, were hiding in hay in their barn while their parents went to a mill. Even so, the two children were captured by Indians and taken to Montreal, Canada, where they spent five years in captivity. In 1761, they were returned to Philadelphia. On June 16, 1761, an ad appeared in Ben Franklin’s _Pennsylvania_ _Gazette_ listing 5 children that were returned to the State House. Nicholas Silvius’s name was on the list.

A year after his return, Nicholas Silvius joined the troops of Captain John Wetherhold in the French and Indian War. Later, records list him as 21 years old, 5’10”, long face, gray eyes, light hair. He served in that company as an Indian scout.

After the French and Indian War, Nicholas Silvius and his two brothers, John and Henry, served in the Revolutionary War and are listed in the Pennsylvania Archives. They fought against the Tories and the Indians. On June 18, 1777, Nicholas is named in a list of returned officers of the 4th Battalion, Militia of Northampton County under Colonel John Sigfreit.

![Image 19](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5388a1dfe4b01656e4f9afa2/5d13a36e-04be-408a-8c7c-275fb200bf34/CC+nicholas.jpg)

A copy of the article as it appeared in 1761 in Benjamin Franklin’s _Pennsylvania Gazette._

**_HOW I DECENDED FROM NICHOLAS SILVIUS, MY 4th GREAT GRANDFATHER:_**

Nicholas Silvius married Anna Mary Catherine Best in 1758. They had 12 children. One of their daughters, Anna Maria, married Wilhelm Bitz in 1803. THEY had 9 children, and one of their daughters, Mary Bitz, married John Varner in Westmoreland County, Pennsylvania.

John Varner was my great, great grandfather. Six of John Varner’s sons left Pennsylvania in the 1850’s and 1860’s to settle on farms near Buffalo, Minnesota. Many of the residents of Wright County are descendants of those six Varner brothers.

Nicholas Silvius died on December 18, 1802. He is buried in the Old Union Cemetery in Greensburg, Westmoreland County, Pennsylvania.

In addition to preparing for the play, with their teacher’s guidance, each student would make some kind of simple gift for their mother. ### MY SALEM WITCH ANCESTOR | NOVEMBER 2025

In researching family history, it is always interesting to come across an ancestor with an unusual life experience. A few years ago, I discovered that my 8th great grandmother was one of the women accused during the Salem Witch Trials.

![Image 24](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5388a1dfe4b01656e4f9afa2/58761bdb-3feb-4356-a352-b6b8667ec347/Salem+1.jpg)

Mary (Perkins) Bradbury was born in England in 1615. She came to New England with her parents in 1630. In 1636, she married Thomas Bradbury, and they had 11 children.

In 1692, she was living in Salisbury, Massachusetts when she was brought to trial for witchcraft. The accusation was made by Richard Carr and his friend who testified that, when they drove their wagon by Mary’s home, they had seen a blue boar come from and reenter her yard and window. Also, Samuel Carr, Richard’s brother, testified that he had seen Mary perched on the capstan of a ship at sea.

Mary was brought to trial, and a written testimony in Mary’s favor was signed by 118 of her friends and neighbors. She pled not guilty, but was brought to trial and convicted on September 9, 1692. She was sentenced with four others to be executed by hanging on September 22, 1692.

Her husband and friends, including her brother, Jacob Perkins, broke her out of the Ipswich jail, and she fled to Amesbury. Mary Bradbury died of natural causes on December 20, 1700 in Salisbury, Essex County, Massachusetts.

In October of 1692, the new Massachusetts Governor Phipps put an end to the witch trials, and any remaining convicted witches had their sentences commuted.

In 1711, the governor of Massachusetts authorized payment to claimants representing 23 persons condemned of witchcraft at Salem. The heirs of Mary Bradbury received a payment of £ 20.

The two of them would often pack up some food for a few days and hike off into the surrounding swamps and woodlands to hunt whatever wild game happened to be in season.

Harry did not say anything to Spencer at the time, and Spencer didn’t say anything to his father.

The next morning, Harry asked Spencer if he had seen the white haze rise from the ground. Spencer agreed that he had seen it, too.

After returning from their hunting trip and relating the event to the rest of their family, they went on with their daily lives. Of course, Harry recounted the incident to his friends in Buffalo, and the tale of ‘seeing a ghost’ was repeated on the street corners and in the saloons around town.

Whenever I heard my father recount the story about seeing his ‘ghost,’ I thought it was just a family tale. Many years later, I was relaying the ghost story to an older family friend. She told me that the story had made the rounds, as she had heard it from some of her neighbors many years ago.

To this day, no one has explained the appearance of that white haze that arose from the ground so many years ago.

The clerk would tear off a length of paper, then place it on the counter, wrap the item, and secure it with tape for the customer. There was also a big spool of string available to wrap up the package for additional security.

On the left side of the drug store was a set of two wooden booths---each one had two bench seats and a table between. Soda drinks and ice cream treats were served there. If I was lucky, I was with my dad, and he would order a chocolate malt for each of us.

Near the front of the store, there was a glass-topped case, lighted on the inside, which contained an enticing collection of warm salted nuts. The display of nuts included peanuts, cashews, pecans, almonds, and others, all arranged loosely in a large divided dish. Grandma would often ask me to buy a small bag of cashews for her. The clerk would open the case, use a scoop to place the nuts in a small bag, then weigh them on a small scale next to the case. I would pay the cashier at the front of the store. Fortunately, Grandma always shared her purchase.

Outside, next to the drugstore entrance was a door that opened to a long staircase. That led to doctors’ offices located in the rooms above the drug store. (Handicapped accessibility was not a priority then.) Dr. Catlin saw patients in one of the rooms; he was later joined by Dr. Sandeen. What I remember best is waiting in the small waiting room and admiring the receptionists. Vivian and Betty were pretty young women who were friendly and efficient in doing their job. I especially remember their beautifully manicured red fingernails.

![Image 31](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5388a1dfe4b01656e4f9afa2/26b7a27c-5ac3-4c1b-9625-942cb5314c85/Drug+Store+Bldg.jpg)

2025 Photograph of the Building

There was another drug store in town located on Highway 25 across from the movie theater, but I only remember it as being very dark and gloomy.

Schmidt’s Drug Store was eventually sold, and was then known for many years as Wagner’s Drug Store. Mr. Wagner made many changes to modernize the store. That building now houses the Forget-Me-Not Café. The upstairs doctors’ offices were removed to a new building on 1st Street South and became known as the Buffalo Clinic. That clinic was later relocated to north Highway 25 and is presently known as Stellis Health.

No one could have imagined the changes that have taken place in drug stores or medical clinics since those of the 1950’s.

### TWO KINDS OF QUILTS | JUNE 2025

In my travels, I have often stopped to admire many beautiful Amish quilts. As a volunteer at the Wright County Historical Society, I have had the privilege of examining some of the historic quilts in our collections. But I have personal experiences with two kinds of quilts.

![Image 32](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5388a1dfe4b01656e4f9afa2/49087d12-488e-4de7-898d-482fe7eb724f/2+quilts+1.jpg)

Modern Day Quilt

**Quilting today:**Many women (and men) find great satisfaction in creating beautiful quilts. We enjoy visiting our favorite quilt shop. Sometimes, we locate a unique pattern, we take hours picking out just the right fabric for that pattern. When we get the fabric home, the process begins---preparing the fabric, locating a place to work, then cutting, cutting, cutting. After that, sewing is the best part---putting those fabric pieces together following pattern directions OR changing the pattern according to some creative whim. It may take months to complete a quilt top and layer the batting and backing. When that is done… “Should I quilt it myself or find someone with a long-arm quilt machine?” Months later, the binding is stitched around the outer edge to finish off the quilt.

**Another Kind of Quilt:**As a child, my family lived in one of those aged farm houses where the walls were lined with old newspapers providing the only insulation. So in the winter, to stay warm, we had several homemade wool quilts for our beds. They were somewhat different than those beautiful Amish quilts, but a lot warmer. Like the Amish quilts, they were put together in layers. The bottom layer was likely an old sheet, or a pieced-together spread of flour sacks or old dresses. The upper layer was also a patchwork of old and used fabric pieces---put together helter-skelter to form a quilt top. Then there was the middle layer---fluffy wool batting about 1 to 2 inches thick. Mom and Grandma would put all three layers together. They’d put the quilt on a quilting frame. Using a large needle and yarn, they’d tie knots every few inches to secure the layers. Sometimes, a cotton binding would be added to finish the edges, but often, the top and bottom layers were just hemmed together to finish the quilt.

![Image 33](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5388a1dfe4b01656e4f9afa2/51197368-44bd-470c-a4f2-bc305805386f/2+quilts+2.jpg)

Patchwork Quilt Top

What about laundering those wool quilts? That was another process. If the quilt was in need of cleaning, the wool lining could not be washed in water. The quilt had to be taken apart. The top and bottom layer could be laundered as usual. If the wool batting was in good condition, it could be re-used, and the quilt would be re-tied.

Wool batting that was dirty or in poor condition was re-cycled. Mom would load the wool into the car, drive to the Cambridge or Faribault Woolen Mills. Someone at the mill would weigh and give her credit on her used wool, and she would purchase a roll of new wool batting for her quilts. Back home, she would repeat the process of layering and tying her quilts.

I enjoyed sleeping under those old wool quilts. They were light weight, exceptionally warm, and the quilt tops always had pieces of fabric reminding me of my old clothes, or my mother’s dresses, or Grandma’s aprons.

Good memories, but I’m glad that polyester batting was invented for our modern-day quilt making.

### THE GRANGE | MAY 2025

![Image 34](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5388a1dfe4b01656e4f9afa2/64faacd4-8ba1-45c0-93b8-41471c14bc2e/Grange+2.jpg)

Oliver H. Kelley

_When I grew up in the 1950’s, my parents were active participants in two organizations: the 4-H Club and the Grange (known officially as the ‘National Grange of the Order of Patrons of Husbandry’)._

In Minnesota, the Grange had branches in many small rural communities. The organization was founded in 1867 by Oliver H. Kelley who had built his home on the Mississippi River just east of Wright County in Sherburne County. His residence is now operated as an active farm by the Minnesota Historical Society and is known as the Kelley Farm.

In Monticello, the Grange included young farmers, older rural residents, a minister’s family, and interested city folks. Monthly Grange meetings began with a secret ritual and included a short business discussion. A substantial lunch and social gathering followed.

Monticello Grange members organized a number of social and community service activities. They regularly scheduled local musicians to play for dances. A professor from St. Cloud State College was hired to teach ballroom dancing prior to a planned evening dance. Occasionally, a caller was booked to teach square dancing.

![Image 35](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5388a1dfe4b01656e4f9afa2/e1358221-18e3-4cf8-8716-cc599b837bb5/Grange+1.jpg)

The Kelley farmhouse

One spring, Grange members advertised a garden-growing contest. It included categories for adults and children; flowers and vegetables. Judges were appointed who toured the gardens late in the season. Small cash prizes were awarded to winners in the various categories.

One year, a retired farmer donated his crop land to the organization as a fundraiser. Members planted and cared for the crops. After harvest, the profits were used for community service programs.

Members of the local Grange occasionally met with others from throughout the region. One summer, several Grange organizations gathered to repair parts of the then-vacant Kelly home. For several years, the local group spent a day manning the Grange booth at the Minnesota State Fair. Another year, I remember helping at a Grange food booth at ‘Plowville USA.’ (At that event, I was able to get an autograph from Hubert H. Humphrey!)

![Image 36](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5388a1dfe4b01656e4f9afa2/394a4741-affe-4a52-9974-cfc72ed2b1ae/Grange+3.jpg)

An environmental issue in the 1950’s included the Sherburne County spring sand storms caused by the barren sandy soil. Grange members united to plant hundreds of evergreen trees in affected areas to prevent erosion from the spring winds.

![Image 37](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5388a1dfe4b01656e4f9afa2/b9d519e9-a5c9-4f24-bd8b-956908d0959c/Grange+4.jpg)

The Grange was not all work. There was plenty of time for good fun. Potluck dinners happened at Ellison Park (then known as Riverside Park). One summer, our family hosted a steak fry in our back yard. On one occasion, the Grange members decided to have a cake-baking contest. A date was set, and several people brought in beautifully decorated cakes. My dad happened to be one of the winners. The cakes were to be part of the lunch. So one of the servers began cutting his cake. Oh-oh, the cake wasn’t cutting…it was a decorated cardboard box!!! Lots of raucous laughter ended the evening.

The Grange no longer exists in the Monticello area, but the organization is still active in other parts of the United States.

As the community grew, other social organizations were formed, Grange members retired or moved away, and the local group dissolved. However, Grange organizations still exist in other parts of the country.

Key issues of the Grange founders:

· Educated farmers on new agricultural practices; inspired the idea for the Agriculture Extension Service

· Supported efforts to regulate railroad rates to transport farm crops

· Protested high interest rates on loans to farmers

· Inspired the idea for the USPS to provide Rural Free Delivery

· Encouraged the U.S. Government to develop the Farm Credit System

### MENZEL’S SERVICE STATION | APRIL 2025

_Who remembers the small corner gas stations where an attendant would pump your gas, wash your windshield and check the oil?_

![Image 38](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5388a1dfe4b01656e4f9afa2/301b4511-62ef-4765-bc11-9e7ce9d901a3/Menzel+1.jpg)

Menzel’s Service Station in downtown Monticello was one of those stations. Martin Menzel, my father-in-law, owned the business, pumped the gas, sold tires, and repaired cars. He opened the business about 1948, and the station closed in the early 1970’s. It was located on the southwest corner of Highway 25 and Broadway. There were three gas pumps, and the driveway was very narrow. Martin had a small office with a canopy over the drive. The office butted up to the neighboring building. There was just enough room inside for a narrow counter, a cash register, a small display of candy bars, and an old red chair for his friends when they stopped in to visit.

![Image 39](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5388a1dfe4b01656e4f9afa2/136d4ec1-8a1a-4f58-86ca-58cee4d78c9d/Menzel+2.jpg)

Attached outside on either side of the office were two restrooms---one for women, one for men. Those restrooms were the only ones available to the public in downtown Monticello, and Martin was diligent in doing regular cleaning. He related the story about accidentally entering the ‘women’s’ to clean while occupied. A woman let out a shriek, and Martin quickly responded, “Sorry, Ma’am, I’m just the janitor!”

Martin kept a green bench near the front of the entry drive. Because it was used by his customers, local shoppers, and anyone out for a walk, the bench was given a new coat of paint every year.

During the early 1950’s, Martin signed a contract with a vendor to sell Christmas trees. Since his was the only location in the city to offer trees, he made a good profit. He put his three sons to work helping people choose ‘just the right tree.’ However, it wasn’t long before other groups opened Christmas tree sales lots, so Martin bowed out.

Another side business for Martin was selling bulk ice. Since Highway 152 was one of the main routes to ‘Up North’, it was busy with travelers to their lake cabins. They needed lots of ice for their coolers and their fresh catch. So Martin asked a friend to build a small ice house with double walls and room for large blocks of ice. He hired a local truck driver to deliver the ice, and again put his three sons to work serving ice customers. The big blocks of ice had to be chopped into chunks to fit their coolers.

Sometime in the 1960’s, Martin discovered that there was a need for a taxi service in the area. So he purchased a used car---a light aqua blue 1957 Chevrolet. He mounted a white TAXI sign on the roof, and placed a series of ads in the local newspaper. For several years, he was the guy to call if your car didn’t start or if you needed to catch the bus at Big Lake. (That ‘57 Chevy was later sold to a local car collector and is still in use.)

Because Highway 152 was well-travelled in the 1950’s and 1960’s, it had an unusually high number of gas stations…around ten at one time. Occasionally, there would be ‘gas wars.’ A station would lower their price for day or two to draw business. As I remember, during that time, the price of gas was around 29 cents a gallon.

![Image 40](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5388a1dfe4b01656e4f9afa2/732ca112-1983-4d8d-868d-a39f456556d4/Menzel+3.jpg)

Martin contracted with DX and later with Gulf Oil to deliver the gasoline. Those companies also offered promotions to attract customers. There were freebies like pencils, rulers, cups, even Teddy bears. For a number of years, Martin offered Gold Bond stamps with each gas purchase.

Martin put many hours into his business. He never employed anyone to assist him. He was known for giving excellent service. If Martin would pump your gas, he would also wash your windshield and check your oil, radiator and tires. I learned to stop in for a gas fill after work. If I stopped before work, I would risk arriving late.

![Image 41](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5388a1dfe4b01656e4f9afa2/7dd20eb6-fb6c-4faf-b2e9-d1da2f0fdf6d/Menzel+4.jpg)

Martin’s sons each put in their time pumping gas and washing windshields. It was a place where their friends could hang out, fix up their cars, help out if needed, and keep an eye out for who was cruising down “Main Street” driving the hottest car.

Most of those small gas stations have closed down now, replaced by the larger convenience/self-service stations.

In Monticello, many people don’t even know there was a gas station on that corner. Highway 25 and Broadway were both expanded, leaving little room for a business venture. The city has developed the corner into a small park. Martin’s shop building served several purposes over the years, but is presently unoccupied.

### SNOWPLOWS OVER THE YEARS | MARCH 2025

One very early morning in the past month, I woke up to hear the familiar roar of the Monticello Township snowplow whizzing by. I thought of how lucky we are to find our roads cleared, often by commuter time.

![Image 42](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5388a1dfe4b01656e4f9afa2/6493471d-93be-4f02-9775-7bf0bd6b14c7/WC+09-060+Carl+Lilja+-+Mail+Carrier+-+Buffalo+Twnshp.jpg)

Carl Lilja’s _Minnesota Special._ Carl was a mail carrier in and around Buffalo Township.

In times past, it took days or weeks to dig out from a heavy snow. In the 1800s, much of that work was done by hand with the help of horses. With the advent of the automobile, some ingenious mechanic figured out a way to attach skis to their car…not to plow, but for a way to navigate the roads.

When I was growing up on the farm, we knew a substantial amount of snow would likely isolate us for a few days. Snowplows were different then. During the 1950’s, there was one man by the name of Alby Perkins who drove the snowplow. He likely never exceeded 10 miles per hour with his plow. With over 52 miles of Monticello Township roads to clear, it must have taken a week or more to complete his job.

![Image 43](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5388a1dfe4b01656e4f9afa2/e792311f-1bfb-40fa-aef3-72c99179235b/Old+Red+Patrol.jpg)

In the late 1960’s, Alby retired. Who could replace him? A local farmer that was well-respected and known for his practical jokes applied for the job. Emil Dorf was hired and became the guy who drove that lofty red machine known as ‘the patrol.’ The patrol was purchased about 1967 to improve the time and effort to clear the roads.

Local residents still tell tales about how snow was cleared in those days. Emil would head out with the patrol. As he made his way around the township roads, he would sometimes spy a gunny sack hanging over a mailbox. It was a signal for that driveway to be cleared (adding time to the route). Sometimes, my dad would watch for the patrol, then walk out to wave Emil in for a coffee or lunch break (adding more time to the route!). Eventually, the roads would be cleared.

![Image 44](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5388a1dfe4b01656e4f9afa2/f2f9fda9-6ac3-40cf-bca7-5d50927b4fce/Monti+Snow+Truck.jpg)

It wasn’t long before there was a need for faster and better road maintenance. Plow trucks were purchased and more workers were hired. Sanding and salting was added to improve road safety.

Today, Monticello Township has two plow trucks for winter road maintenance. They keep a vintage model as a spare in case of mechanical problems. That’s a big improvement over Emil’s ungainly contraption! However, that old red patrol is still in use. It’s kept up for occasional grading on the few gravel roads still in existence, but is no longer used for snow removal.

### THE PITCHER & BOWL | FEBRUARY 2025

This is a story of how two family heirlooms, separated for over 70 years, finally have been reunited.

![Image 45](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5388a1dfe4b01656e4f9afa2/96b9ee50-2ef2-42e8-89ed-f13aa10085ac/CC+-+Pitcher.jpg)

During the Depression years, many young families occupied rental farmhouses in rural Wright County. A family might stay for a few years before purchasing a farm of their own. This was the circumstance for Rudolph and Mabel Lundquist. They rented an 80-acre farm between Monticello and Buffalo on what is now County Road 37. The farmhouse had no electricity, no running water, and no central heat. When they left that farm, they took what belongings they had with them. That included a pretty china washbowl and soap dish.

Another family, the Williams’, soon moved in, also renting from the absentee owner. They occupied the farmhouse for several years during the early 1940’s. They noticed that a large pretty china pitcher had been left in the house.

In 1946, my parents, Spencer and Mabel Kopff, purchased the farm. My father, being a carpenter, did some much-needed repair work on the farmhouse. But it was still without central heat, water, or electricity. The Kopffs made friends with the Williams family who helped with the move. The pretty China pitcher was still in the farmhouse and the Williams family did not claim it, so it became one of Mabel Kopff’s possessions.

As time went on, the bowl and soap dish became a family heirloom for Mabel Lundquist, and she eventually passed it on down to her daughter, Audrey Murray. A similar progression happened in the Kopff family. Mabel gifted the pitcher to her daughter, Claudia Menzel.

![Image 46](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5388a1dfe4b01656e4f9afa2/5305d88b-97a5-4ee7-a61c-40842043241a/Pitcher+and+Bowl+2.jpg)

Because the Lundquists and the Kopffs were long-time friends, the _“Bowl and Pitcher”_ story became a topic of conversation. In the mid-1990’s, a Lundquist granddaughter, Amy Murray, contacted Claudia. Her purpose was to obtain the pitcher as a surprise for Audrey, her mother. Claudia was not ready to give up her family heirloom.

After Claudia arrived home, she thought about the bowl and pitcher being separated for over 70 years, and decided that it was time that they were reunited. So she contacted Amy, offered the pitcher to the Murray family, and the exchange was made. Hopefully, the bowl and pitcher set will remain family heirlooms for future generations.
